claims.text: Free-energy landscape sampling using umbrella sampling or metadynamics coupled with kinetic modeling can precisely control phase evolution in thermally processed Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs.
The proposed approach will reduce unwanted phase segregation relative to conventional processing.
Cast or homogenized Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs can contain multiple constituent phases.
Free-energy landscape sampling can map the barriers for phase nucleation and growth in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs.
Predicted free-energy profiles can be used to optimize processing temperature, annealing time, and cooling rate.
Free-energy barriers govern the nucleation and growth kinetics of constituent phases.
Accurate free-energy sampling predicts critical phase-transformation barriers.
Knowledge of transformation barriers permits thermal treatments to selectively favor desired-phase nucleation.
Barrier-informed thermal treatments can suppress formation of deleterious phases.
The proposed route will produce a lower fraction of unwanted phases than empirically optimized thermal processing.
The proposed route will improve phase uniformity relative to traditional processing.
Conventional arc melting, isothermal annealing, and slow cooling generally cause uncontrolled phase transformations and undesirable phase mixtures.
Complex multicomponent interactions may limit predictive phase control during large-scale industrial processing.
The effectiveness of phase control may vary with compositional fluctuations in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs.
Computational free-energy methods have demonstrated promising efficiency and accuracy for multicomponent HEAs.
The quantitative predictive accuracy of free-energy landscape sampling for Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni phase evolution remains experimentally unvalidated.
XRD peak analysis can quantify phase fractions during comparison of the two processing routes.
TEM can be used to observe nucleation sites and phase-growth rates during processing.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant reduction in unwanted phases or failure to reproduce predicted kinetics would falsify the hypothesis.
